before: A constructor runs when new creates an instance. It has the same name as the class and no return type—not even void.
new Counter(4) passes 4 to the constructor parameter start. Score = start stores that input in the new object’s field.

The constructor executes for each new object. Supplying a different input to a later creation does not reinitialize an earlier object. After declaring this one-argument constructor, an empty new Counter() call is not supplied automatically.
Expected behavior from this example: 4 then 7. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Give Counter a second constructor input for a label and initialize both fields. Use a .NET 10 console project with C# 14; reading completion does not verify this local work.
after: A constructor is code that sets up an object when new creates it. Here, it sets the new counter's starting score.
A constructor has the same name as its class. It has no return type, not even void.
new Counter(4) sends 4 to the start parameter. Score = start stores that value in the new object's field.
The program prints 4, then 7. Each object's constructor stores the input supplied for that object.
Creating a later object does not reset an earlier one. This class declares only a constructor with one input, so callers must supply that input; C# does not also add an empty constructor.
